provenance.method: Static team-labelled source references, independently checked against the identified downloaded source bytes before the expanded benchmark freeze.
provenance.excerpt_normalization: HTML: stdlib HTMLParser text nodes excluding scripts/styles, joined with spaces then whitespace collapsed. Exact contiguous excerpts are individually enumerated and joined with blank lines. Locations use Unicode character offsets, zero-based and end-exclusive.
provenance.retrieved_at_note: No timestamp asserted; source bytes identified by SHA-256.
provenance.split_policy: Publisher/source-family split: both NHLBI DASH pages are dev; all NIDDK pages are test. No KDIGO included. Parent must preserve these family assignments when merging. Test is not a claim of freedom from pretraining or unrecorded exposure.
provenance.source_check: All six original HTML SHA-256 hashes and all 61 excerpt substrings and offsets independently checked against downloaded bytes. Extraction and AnswerDraft schemas, predicate evaluation, source links, splits and lexical exemplars checked locally.
provenance.pattern_checks: Bounded lexical diagnostics only; preserve semantic qualifiers and source scope. Ten answerable questions selected for evidence-removal ablation: four dev and six test.
provenance.experiment_context: The main 14-passage experiment was already run as an initial experiment. No prompts were tuned from its outputs. This expanded-reference check used source text and local schemas, with no evaluation model calls.

Based on these recommendations, the following table shows examples of daily and weekly servings that meet DASH eating plan targets for a 2,000-calorie-a-day diet. Food Group Daily Servings Grains 6–8 Meats, poultry, and fish 6 or less Vegetables 4–5 Fruit 4–5 Low-fat or fat-free dairy products 2–3 Fats and oils 2–3 Sodium 2,300 mg* Weekly Servings Nuts, seeds, dry beans, and peas 4–5 Sweets 5 or less *1,500 milligrams (mg) sodium lowers blood pressure even further than 2,300 mg sodium daily.

excerpts.text: Following DASH

To figure out your calorie needs, you need to consider your age and physical activity level. If you want to maintain your current weight, you should eat only as many calories as you burn by being physically active. This is called energy balance. (For more information about energy balance, go to the Health Topics Overweight and Obesity article.) If you need to lose weight, you should eat fewer calories than you burn or increase your activity level to burn more calories than you eat.

excerpts.text: Healthy Living with Diabetes

The plate method helps you control portion sizes without counting and measuring. This method divides a 9-inch plate into the following three sections to help you choose the types and amounts of foods to eat for each meal. Nonstarchy vegetables—such as leafy greens, peppers, carrots, or green beans—should make up half of your plate. Carb foods that are high in fiber—such as brown rice, whole grains, beans, or fruits—should make up one-quarter of your plate. Protein foods—such as lean meats, fish, dairy, or tofu or other soy products—should make up one quarter of your plate. If you are not taking insulin, you may not need to count carbs when using the plate method.

Tips to reduce phosphorus in your diet include Limit or avoid packaged and processed foods and drinks that have added phosphorus, such as deli meats, flavored drinks, and other processed foods. Check Nutrition Facts labels for added phosphorus. Look for “phosphorus” or words with “PHOS,” such as phosphoric acid, disodium phosphate, and monosodium phosphate on the ingredient list. Eat larger portions of fruits and vegetables, which are naturally low in phosphorus, and smaller portions of foods high in phosphorus. Keep in mind, your body absorbs more phosphorus from animal-based foods, such as meat and poultry, than from plant-based foods, such as beans and seeds. Some packaged meats and poultry have added phosphorus. Ask someone who works in the meat department to show you which meats do not have added phosphorus.

If your potassium level is high, your health care professional may recommend you Limit serving sizes of foods that contain potassium. Keep in mind that a large serving of a lower-potassium food may have more potassium than a small serving of a higher-potassium food. Use spices and herbs instead of salt substitutes, which can be high in potassium. Limit foods with potassium chloride on the ingredient list. Potassium chloride is sometimes used in place of salt in some packaged foods. Drain canned fruits and vegetables and throw out the liquid, which is often high in potassium. Use food preparation and cooking methods, such as boiling and leaching, that can lower the amount of potassium in certain vegetables.

Get enough calcium from foods Even though calcium sounds like it would be the cause of calcium stones, it’s not. In the right amounts, calcium can block other substances in the digestive tract that may cause stones. Talk with a health care professional about how much calcium you should eat to help prevent getting more calcium oxalate stones and to support strong bones. It may be best to get calcium from low-oxalate, plant-based foods such as calcium-fortified juices, cereals, breads, some kinds of vegetables, and some types of beans. Ask a dietitian or other health care professional which foods are the best sources of calcium for you.

questions.question: Does DASH require special foods, and which food groups does it emphasize?

reference_answer.answer: DASH requires no special foods. It emphasizes vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fat-free or low-fat dairy, fish, poultry, beans, nuts and vegetable oils, while limiting saturated-fat foods and sugar-sweetened beverages and sweets.

questions.question: How may dialysis change protein needs, and which modality removes more protein according to NIDDK?

reference_answer.answer: Dialysis may increase protein needs because treatment removes protein. The amount depends on modality; peritoneal dialysis removes more protein than hemodialysis.

questions.question: Which foods should be included when counting liquid intake during hemodialysis?

reference_answer.answer: Count foods such as soup, gelatin, pudding and ice cream, plus water-containing fruits and vegetables such as melons, grapes, tomatoes and lettuce; do not count only drinks.

questions.question: What fluid advice is given for stone prevention, and which exclusion accompanies the six-to-eight-glass recommendation?

reference_answer.answer: Drink enough liquid, mainly water. Many health professionals recommend six to eight 8-ounce glasses a day unless there is kidney failure; discuss the individual amount with a health professional.

reference_answer.answer: It applies to people who have had calcium oxalate stones. The wording is that they may want to avoid those foods, along with nuts/nut products and peanuts, and discuss oxalate intake with a health professional.

questions.question: Does the calcium oxalate stone guidance imply avoiding dietary calcium?

reference_answer.answer: No. In the right amounts, calcium can block substances in the digestive tract that may cause stones. Discuss the amount and suitable sources with a professional; low-oxalate plant-based calcium sources may be best.
